summary: Sirach 10 begins with rulers and judges, saying a leader's understanding or lack of discipline affects a whole people. It then attacks pride by stressing human mortality, God's power to overturn rulers and nations, and the greater honor of those who fear the Lord. The chapter closes by weighing honor, poverty, riches, wisdom, work, humility, and self-respect.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers several major concerns of Sirach: public authority, humility before God, and the danger of judging worth by status or wealth. It shows wisdom as something tested both in government and in ordinary social ranking.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Composed in Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule and translated in Egypt, in a world where Jewish scribal learning existed within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean setting.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction using compact poetic sayings, paired lines, direct address, and social teaching.

outline.heading: Leadership shapes a people
outline.note: Wise rule orders a people and a city, while the chapter also says government, prosperity, and honor are in the Lord's hand.

outline.heading: Pride, anger, and mortality
outline.note: The teacher warns against anger and violence, calls pride hateful, and undercuts pride by pointing to bodily decay and death.

outline.heading: Pride as departure from the Lord
outline.note: Pride is described as beginning when a person departs from the Lord, and the Lord is depicted as overthrowing rulers and nations.

outline.heading: Honor belongs to those who fear the Lord
outline.note: The chapter compares honor among offspring, rulers, rich and poor people, and says none is greater than the one who fears the Lord.

outline.heading: Work, humility, and measured honor
outline.note: The closing sayings warn against boasting, commend labor and humility, and compare honor and dishonor in poverty and riches.

keyVerses.text: The government of the earth is in the Lord’s hand. In due time, he will raise up over it the right person at the right time.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the opening section by placing political authority under God's control without spelling out every historical case.

keyVerses.text: Pride is hateful before the Lord and men. Arrogance is abhorrent in the judgment of both.
keyVerses.why: This states the chapter's central moral warning in direct terms.

keyVerses.text: The Lord cast down the thrones of rulers and set the lowly in their place.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter's strongest image of reversed status: rulers brought down and the lowly raised.

keyVerses.text: The prince, the judge, and the mighty man will be honored. There is not one of them greater than he who fears the Lord.
keyVerses.why: This summarizes the chapter's ranking of honor: public office matters, but fear of the Lord is greater.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with judges, officials, rulers, and kings?
questions.answer: The opening sayings focus on public leadership because a ruler's character affects more than the ruler alone. Verse 2 says officials and residents reflect the judge or ruler, and verse 3 contrasts an undisciplined king with understanding among the powerful.

questions.question: Does verse 4 mean every ruler is directly approved by God?
questions.answer: The verse says government is in the Lord's hand and that the right person is raised up in due time. It does not explain how every ruler's rise should be evaluated, and the same chapter criticizes injustice, violence, greed, and undisciplined kings. Responsible readers therefore should not use this verse alone to approve any ruler's conduct.

questions.question: What does “scribe” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the scribe is a person who receives honor from the Lord's hand. Ben Sira was himself a Jerusalem teacher and scribe, but verse 5 only says that honor is laid upon the person of the scribe; it does not give a job description inside the verse.

questions.question: How are anger, violence, pride, and arrogance connected?
questions.answer: Verses 6-7 move from everyday conduct toward a deeper disposition. The reader is told not to be angry with a neighbor for every wrong and to do nothing by violence; then pride and arrogance are named as hateful and abhorrent. The chapter treats destructive actions and inflated self-importance as related dangers.

questions.question: Why does the chapter talk about dirt, ashes, maggots, vermin, and worms?
questions.answer: These images press the point that human beings are mortal and bodily fragile. The king of today dies tomorrow, and the dead person is described in terms of decay. The argument is not scientific explanation; it is wisdom rhetoric against pride.

questions.question: What is the “beginning of pride” in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says pride begins when a person departs from the Lord, and verse 13 says the beginning of pride is sin. The chapter describes pride not merely as confidence or social awkwardness, but as a turning away from the one who made the person.

questions.question: Why is verse 21 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verse 21 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying poor people are always wiser than rich people?
questions.answer: No. Verse 23 says not to dishonor a poor man who has understanding, and not to glorify a sinner. Verse 30 says a poor man can be honored for knowledge and a rich man for riches, while verse 31 complicates both poverty and riches by asking how honor or dishonor carries across conditions.

questions.question: How can someone “glorify your soul in humility”?
questions.answer: The phrase holds together humility and appropriate self-respect. Verse 28 tells the son to ascribe honor according to worthiness, while verse 26 warns against flaunting wisdom or boasting. The chapter does not praise self-contempt; it rejects pride while allowing measured honor.

glossary.def: A public decision-maker whose wisdom or lack of wisdom affects the people under his authority.
People serving under a judge or ruler; verse 2 says their character follows the pattern of the one who governs.
A learned person associated here with honor from the Lord's hand; in Sirach's wider setting, scribes are connected with study and instruction.
The chapter's name for an arrogant departure from the Lord, treated as hateful and destructive.
People of humble or reduced status whom the Lord is depicted as setting in the place of rulers and nations.
The chapter's repeated marker of true honor, greater than rank, wealth, or public power.
